questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Northgate Media, a news publisher with a national site and 12 regional editions, uses Claude Code to accelerate development in its monorepo (a Next.js front end, a Django CMS, and a Go service that ingests wire-agency feeds). Its 35 developers use it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, through team slash commands and CLAUDE.md files, and they have to decide when to use plan mode versus direct execution. Since last Tuesday's release, newsletter sign-ups from article pages have dropped 38%, and nobody knows why. A developer proposes running Claude Code through a fixed five-step prompt chain: check the signup form, then the API endpoint, then the database writes, then the email-service integration, then write a summary. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt the chain, because a fixed order makes the investigation deterministic and guarantees that each layer of the stack is examined exactly once.
Adopt the chain but run the five steps in parallel, so that the investigation finishes sooner while still covering every layer of the stack.
Replace the chain with one prompt that lists all five layers as a checklist, so that Claude sees the whole investigation plan from the start.
Prefer dynamic decomposition: let each next step follow from what the previous one found, since the cause is unknown and may lie elsewhere.
questoes.explicacao: The cause of the drop is unknown, so this is an open-ended investigation: what Claude finds at each step (for example, that sign-ups reach the API but no email is sent) should decide the next subtask. Fixed prompt chains fit predictable, repeatable work whose steps are known in advance; for an investigation, dynamic adaptive decomposition avoids spending steps on layers the evidence has cleared and can follow leads the chain never planned for.
feedbacks: Reproducibility is a real benefit of prompt chaining, which is why it fits predictable multi-aspect reviews. Here the cause is unknown: a fixed order spends steps on layers the evidence has already cleared and cannot follow a lead outside the five planned steps (for example, an A/B-test flag or a CDN rule).

Parallelism speeds things up but keeps the same flaw: the subtasks are fixed in advance instead of being generated from intermediate findings, so the investigation still cannot adapt to what it discovers.

A single checklist prompt is still a predefined plan; it only changes how the plan is delivered. The problem is not visibility of the steps but that, in an investigation, the next step should depend on what was just found.
Correct. An open-ended investigation calls for adaptive decomposition, where subtasks are generated from what each step uncovers.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer asked Claude Code to find every caller of the legacy `sanitize_html()` before deleting it. Claude grepped for `sanitize_html`, found 4 call sites, and the deletion broke 11 templates in staging: `cms/text_utils.py` re-exports the function as `clean_body` and `strip_markup`, and the templates import those names. Next sprint the team will delete `render_byline()`, which also sits behind wrapper modules, and wants the search to be complete without reading the repository's 9,000 files. Which approach should Claude follow?
opcoes: Grep for `render_byline`, then Read every module that imports anything from a utils package, so that indirect uses are found by inspecting those files.
Use Glob to list every `*_utils.py` and `wrappers/**` file and Read each one in full, so that all wrapper modules are understood before deleting.
First identify every name under which wrapper modules export `render_byline` (aliases, re-exports), then Grep the codebase for each of those names.
Grep for `render_byline` plus a case-insensitive search for the word "byline", so that renamed and aliased call sites are caught with direct ones.
questoes.explicacao: Wrappers hide a function behind other names, so a search for the original name misses every caller that imports an alias. The reliable method is to first enumerate the names the wrapper modules export for the function, then Grep the whole codebase for each one. That stays targeted and complete without reading thousands of files.
feedbacks: Reading every module that imports from a utils package can find indirect uses, but it is the "read everything" approach the team wants to avoid, and it still depends on spotting the aliases by eye.

Understanding the wrapper modules is the right instinct, but reading them is only half the job: without then searching the codebase for each exported alias, the callers in templates are still not found.
Correct. Enumerate the exported names first, then search for each one; this traces usage through wrapper modules.

A keyword search is cheap and catches some renames, but aliases need not contain the original word (the last incident involved `clean_body` and `strip_markup`). It would miss those and add many irrelevant hits.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, the team wants Claude Code to read and update tickets in the company's standard Jira Cloud instance, open pull requests on GitHub, and query "Rundown", an in-house editorial planning system that tracks which stories are scheduled for each edition. A developer proposes writing three custom MCP servers this sprint so that the team controls every tool. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Build one custom MCP server that wraps Jira, GitHub, and Rundown behind a unified set of tools, so that Claude sees one consistent interface.
Use maintained community servers for the two standard tools, and write a custom server only for the editorial planning system.
Skip MCP for Jira and GitHub and let Claude call their REST APIs with curl through Bash, building an MCP server only for Rundown.
Build custom servers for all three systems first, so that tool names and descriptions follow one convention, and evaluate community servers later.
questoes.explicacao: Jira and GitHub are standard integrations with maintained community MCP servers, so building them from scratch duplicates work and adds maintenance. Custom servers are worth building for team-specific systems like Rundown, which no community server covers. This gets the integrations working fastest with the least code to own.
feedbacks: One interface sounds tidy, but it means re-implementing two standard integrations and coupling them to an in-house one; a change in any of the three systems now touches a single custom server the team must maintain.
Correct. Use community servers for standard integrations and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows.
Raw curl through Bash works, but it gives Claude no typed tools or descriptions for Jira and GitHub, makes each call improvised, and ignores ready-made servers that already do this well.
Consistent naming is a reasonable goal, but it does not justify writing and maintaining servers that already exist; descriptions can be reviewed without re-implementing the integrations.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer asks Claude Code to update every Storybook story for the article-card components. Stories sit next to their components across dozens of folders and follow the naming pattern `ArticleCard*.stories.tsx`. The session log shows that Claude ran Grep for "ArticleCard" across the repository, received 1,400 matching lines from components, tests, CSS modules, and docs, and began reading files one by one. Which way of locating the files is the better choice here?
opcoes: Grep for "ArticleCard" only in files that also contain "Meta" or "storiesOf", so that only the files that define stories are returned.
Read the Storybook main configuration and follow its story globs and imports, so that only the stories Storybook registers are updated.
Grep for "ArticleCard" and then filter the matches by file extension, so that hits in CSS modules and docs are discarded before reading.
Use Glob with a pattern such as `**/ArticleCard*.stories.tsx`, because the target files are identified by their names, not their contents.
questoes.explicacao: The files to change are defined by a naming pattern, so this is a file-path problem: Glob matches paths by name or extension and returns exactly the story files. Grep searches file contents and is the right tool for finding callers, messages, or imports, which is why it produced 1,400 noisy lines here.
feedbacks: Refining a content search can narrow the hits, but it still treats a naming problem as a content problem; it depends on how each story is written and returns line matches instead of a list of files.
Following the configuration is a reasonable way to understand Storybook, but it adds reading and interpretation when the files can be found directly from their name pattern.
Filtering by extension removes some noise, yet components and tests share the .tsx extension, so the result is still a long list of content matches rather than the story files.
Correct. Glob is for finding files by path pattern; Grep is for searching inside files.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer spent Monday in a Claude Code session analyzing the comments module and agreeing moderation thresholds with the editors. On Tuesday, a teammate's merged PR rewrote 23 of the 31 files that session had read, including the data model. When she resumes Monday's session, Claude proposes edits that call `score_comment_v1()`, which no longer exists. Wednesday's work must be based on the current code without losing Monday's conclusions. What should she change?
opcoes: Keep resuming Monday's session but start with "the code has changed, re-check before editing", so that Claude re-validates its assumptions as it works.
Resume the session and run /compact first, so that the stale tool output is condensed and takes up less room than the new file reads.
Resume the session and have Claude re-read all 31 files right away, so that the current contents are loaded before any further edits are planned.
Start a new session seeded with a summary of Monday's conclusions and agreed decisions, and let Claude read the current code it needs.
questoes.explicacao: Most of the files the session read have changed, so its tool results are stale and keep pulling Claude toward code that no longer exists. Starting fresh with a structured summary of the conclusions keeps what is still valid (the agreed thresholds) and lets Claude read the current code. Resuming is the better choice only when the prior context is mostly still valid.
feedbacks: A general warning does not tell Claude which of its earlier observations are wrong; the outdated file contents stay in context and keep influencing its proposals.
/compact replaces the history with a summary of that history, so the stale observations about removed functions are summarized and carried forward rather than removed.

Re-reading helps, but the 31 old tool results stay in the resumed history next to the new ones, so Claude must reconcile two versions of most files. With 23 of 31 files changed, a fresh start is cleaner.
Correct. When prior tool results are mostly stale, a new session with an injected summary is more reliable than resuming.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer is migrating image resizing to a new service in three phases: discover every place that generates image renditions (about 70 files across templates, CDN config, and Celery tasks), design the new approach, then implement it. In a first attempt in a single Claude Code session, discovery filled the context with thousands of lines of search output, and by the implementation phase Claude had lost track of design decisions. Which two actions best prevent this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Use a model with a larger context window for this migration, so that all three phases fit in one conversation without losing earlier details.
Run the discovery phase in the Explore subagent, so that its verbose search output stays there and only a summary reaches the main session.
Run each phase in its own session and paste the complete transcript of the previous phase into the first prompt of the next session, so nothing is lost.
Ask Claude to run its searches with fewer context lines and shorter output, so that discovery adds less text to the main conversation.
Before designing, condense the discovery findings into a short list of files and call sites, and carry only that summary into the next phase.
questoes.explicacao: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery: thousands of lines of search output stay in its context, and the main conversation receives a summary. Carrying a condensed summary of one phase's findings into the next keeps later phases focused on what matters. Together they keep the main context free for the design decisions that implementation depends on.
feedbacks: A larger window delays the problem but does not solve it: verbose output still competes with the design decisions for attention, and details in the middle of a long context are easy to lose.
Correct. The Explore subagent keeps verbose discovery output out of the main conversation and returns a summary.
Separate sessions are a good idea, but pasting full transcripts re-imports all the verbose discovery output into the next phase, recreating the original problem.
Trimming output helps at the margin, but discovery over about 70 files still accumulates in the main context; the output needs to be isolated, not just shortened.
Correct. Summarizing one phase's key findings before starting the next keeps only what later phases need in context.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer is trying out an experimental MCP server that queries her personal analytics notebook, a prototype only she uses. She added it to the repository's `.mcp.json` and merged the change. The next morning, 14 teammates were prompted by Claude Code to approve an unknown "lena-analytics" server, and CI logs show failed connections to `localhost:8899`. What is the flaw in how this server was configured?
opcoes: Her experimental server should have been declared in the project CLAUDE.md with its start command, so Claude launches it only for analytics.
A server only she uses belongs in user scope (`~/.claude.json`), not in a project file that every clone of the repository picks up.
The entry should use `${ANALYTICS_URL}` expansion instead of a hard-coded localhost URL, so that each teammate can point it at their own instance.
It should have been added to `.mcp.json` on a long-lived feature branch, so that teammates receive it only after the experiment has been reviewed.
questoes.explicacao: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is for shared team tooling: it is committed, and every clone (including CI) picks it up. Personal or experimental servers belong in the user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, where they affect only the person who configured them.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.md holds instructions and context; it is not where MCP servers are configured or started, so this would not make the server available at all.
Correct. Personal or experimental servers go in user scope (`~/.claude.json`); shared team servers go in the project `.mcp.json`.
Environment variable expansion is the right tool for credentials and endpoints in shared servers, but this server is not meant to be shared; teammates have no instance to point it at.
Keeping it on a branch delays the problem rather than fixing the scope: once merged, every clone still receives a server that only one person uses.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, the team's MCP server for the CMS exposes the tools `list_sections`, `search_articles`, and `get_table_info`. Traces show that Claude spends 6 to 10 calls at the start of most tasks just discovering which content types, section taxonomies, and database tables exist before doing any real work. Which two changes would most reduce these exploratory calls? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Paste the current section taxonomy and table list into the project CLAUDE.md, so that every session already has them without any calls.
Expose the latest `search_articles` results as an MCP resource refreshed every minute, so that Claude reads recent articles instead of searching.
Add a `discover_everything` tool that returns all sections, content types, and tables at once, so that exploration takes a single call.
Expose the content-type definitions and the section taxonomy as MCP resources, so that Claude can see what exists without first calling a tool.
Expose the CMS database schema as an MCP resource describing tables and columns, so that Claude consults it instead of probing with calls.
questoes.explicacao: MCP resources are the mechanism for exposing content catalogs such as documentation hierarchies, taxonomies, and database schemas. They give the agent visibility into what data exists without exploratory tool calls, while tools remain for actions and queries. Content types, the section taxonomy, and the schema are exactly such catalogs.
feedbacks: Static copies in CLAUDE.md load into every session, including unrelated ones, and go stale as editors add sections; the server can publish the live catalog instead.
Search results are the output of a query, not a catalog of what exists; Claude would still need search to find specific articles, so the discovery calls remain.
Fewer calls, but still an exploratory tool call on every task, and one that dumps every catalog into context whether it is relevant or not.
Correct. A catalog of content types and sections is what MCP resources are for.
Correct. Exposing the schema as a resource removes the probing calls used to discover tables.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer has a named Claude Code session, "paywall-metering", in which Claude mapped how the paywall counts free articles. Over the weekend, the only change to that code was a constant in `metering/config.py`: `FREE_ARTICLES_PER_MONTH` went from 5 to 4. A teammate proposes a rule that every investigation should start a fresh session each morning, seeded with a summary, "to avoid stale context". How should you evaluate the proposal for this case?
opcoes: Agree: a fresh session seeded with a summary is always more reliable than resuming, because any resumed session may contain stale tool results.
Disagree here: resume with `--resume paywall-metering` and tell Claude that `metering/config.py` changed, so that it re-reads only that file.
Agree, and have Claude re-read every file from Friday at the start of the fresh session, so that its new context matches the current code exactly.
Disagree: resume the named session as it is, since a single changed constant is too small to affect any of Claude's conclusions about metering.
questoes.explicacao: Resuming is the better choice when the prior context is mostly valid; here one constant changed and everything else Claude learned still holds. Resuming the named session and pointing Claude to the specific changed file enables targeted re-analysis without repeating the whole exploration. A fresh start with a summary is for cases where most prior tool results are stale.
feedbacks: Fresh sessions with summaries are the right call when prior tool results are largely stale, not in every case. Here the rule would discard a valid, detailed analysis because of one constant.
Correct. Mostly valid context favors resuming, and telling Claude which file changed enables targeted re-analysis.
This combines the cost of a fresh start with a full re-exploration: it discards valid context and then rebuilds it.
Resuming is right, but not telling Claude about the change leaves its old reading of `config.py` in context, and that constant drives the counting logic it mapped.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, after a 50-minute Claude Code session that mapped the article-rendering pipeline (templates, cache layers, CDN purge rules), a developer wants to compare two refactoring approaches: server rendering with edge caching versus incremental static regeneration. She must not repeat the 50-minute analysis, the two explorations must not influence each other, and the original analysis must stay intact for a possible third option. What should she do?
opcoes: Explore the first approach in the same session, then tell Claude to set it aside and explore the second, so that both build on the full analysis.
Open two new sessions and paste a summary of the pipeline mapping into each one, so that the two explorations start clean and stay separate.
Have Claude explore both approaches in the same session, alternating steps under labeled headings, so that they can be compared side by side.
Fork the session at the end of the analysis into two branches, one per approach, so that each starts from the same baseline without seeing the other.
questoes.explicacao: Forking a session (fork_session) creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline. Each branch inherits the full 50-minute analysis, the branches do not see each other's exploration, and the original session remains available for a later third branch.
feedbacks: Reusing the analysis is good, but the second exploration inherits everything said about the first; "set it aside" does not remove that context, so the comparison is biased.
Separate sessions avoid cross-contamination, but a pasted summary is a lossy copy of the analysis; the detailed tool results behind it are gone, so some re-exploration is likely.
Interleaving keeps both approaches in one context, so each influences the other; labels organize the output but do not isolate the reasoning.
Correct. fork_session gives independent branches from a shared baseline and leaves the original intact.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer new to publishing must add embargo support: articles with an embargo time must not appear in RSS feeds, sitemaps, site search, push alerts, or partner syndication until the embargo lifts, across time zones. Similar features have shipped with gaps found only in production, such as a cached sitemap exposing a story early. He is about to ask Claude Code to "implement embargo support". What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Have Claude interview him first about caching, delivery timing, edge cases, and failure modes, before any of the code gets written.
Have Claude implement the feature and then write tests for it, so that any gaps show up as failing tests before the change is merged.
Enter plan mode and have Claude write a step-by-step implementation plan covering each of the five surfaces named in the ticket.
Write a detailed embargo specification himself from the ticket and hand it to Claude, so that the work follows one precise source.
questoes.explicacao: In an unfamiliar domain, the biggest risk is the considerations nobody wrote down (cache invalidation, time-zone boundaries, partner delivery delays). The interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface them before implementation starts. Planning or testing only covers what the developer already knows to ask for.
feedbacks: Correct. The interview pattern surfaces design considerations the developer may not have anticipated, before implementation.
Tests written after the implementation, from the same understanding, cover the cases already imagined; the production gaps came from cases nobody imagined.
Plan mode is useful for exploring the code and designing changes, but a plan built from the ticket's five surfaces inherits the ticket's blind spots, such as cached sitemaps.
A precise spec helps, but he lacks the domain knowledge to write it completely; the missing considerations are exactly what his spec would leave out.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer has spent three days with Claude Code investigating why regional sites show stale headlines. Early on, Claude established specifics: `HeadlineCache` has a 900-second TTL in `regional/settings.py`, and the purge webhook skips sites with `is_syndicated=True`. After several long sessions, Claude now answers follow-up questions with "typical cache invalidation issues" instead of these findings. Which approach best keeps the findings available as the investigation continues?
opcoes: Run /compact regularly, since the summary it produces carries the key findings forward and frees space for the rest of the investigation.
Resume the first day's session with --resume each morning, so that every finding from that day stays in the conversation history.
Add the findings to the project CLAUDE.md, since that file is loaded into every session and the findings would always be in context.
Have Claude keep a findings file in the repository, such as `notes/stale-headlines.md`, and consult it before answering new questions.
questoes.explicacao: Context degrades in long investigations: the model drifts toward generic patterns instead of the specific classes and values it found earlier. A scratchpad file that Claude writes key findings to, and re-reads before answering, persists those facts across compactions and sessions without polluting shared configuration.
feedbacks: /compact helps with context size, but each summary is lossy: exact values such as the 900-second TTL are the details most likely to be condensed into generalities.
Resuming keeps the history, but that history is what is degrading; the original findings sit deep in a long context where they are easy to overlook.
CLAUDE.md is shared team configuration loaded for everyone in every session; one developer's investigation notes do not belong there and would add noise for the whole team.
Correct. A scratchpad file persists key findings across context boundaries and can be consulted on demand.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, `feeds/builders.py` contains five identical blocks, one per feed type: `except CacheMiss:` followed by `return None`. Claude Code must change only the third block, for the podcast feed, so that it raises `FeedUnavailable` instead. Edit fails each time with an error saying that the text matches 5 locations. The other four blocks must stay unchanged. What should Claude do?
opcoes: Read the full file, then use Write to save the complete contents with only the third block changed, so that the result does not depend on a match.
Run Edit with `replace_all` enabled, then restore the four unintended changes with further Edit calls, so that only the third block differs.
Run a Bash `sed` command that targets the third occurrence of the pattern, so that the change is applied in place without any anchor text.
Ask the developer to add a unique comment above the third block, so that Edit has distinct anchor text to match on its next attempt.
questoes.explicacao: Edit needs unique anchor text; when the target text appears several times, the reliable fallback is to Read the whole file and Write the full updated content. This makes the change predictable and leaves the other blocks exactly as they were.
feedbacks: Correct. When Edit cannot find a unique match, Read + Write is the reliable fallback.
replace_all changes every block, and reverting four of them hits the same problem: those blocks are identical again, so the reverting Edit calls cannot target them uniquely either.
A sed command counting occurrences can work, but it is fragile (a later change that adds a similar block shifts the count) and bypasses the built-in file tools without need.
This shifts work to the developer for something Claude can do itself, and adding comments only to create anchors changes the code for the tool's convenience.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, each Django app keeps its migrations in its own folder, such as `apps/articles/migrations/` and `apps/comments/migrations/`. The team created `.claude/rules/migrations.md` ("never edit applied migrations; always define reverse operations") with this frontmatter: `paths: ["migrations/*.py"]`. When developers edit migration files, Claude ignores these conventions, while the other rule files in the same folder work as expected. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: Rule files load only when the root CLAUDE.md references them with @import, and this file was never imported by the root CLAUDE.md.
The rule is written as prohibitions, and Claude tends to skip negative instructions, so the conventions should be restated as positive steps.
The glob matches only a `migrations/` folder at the repository root; a pattern such as `**/migrations/*.py` is needed to match each app.
The frontmatter lacks a `description` field, which Claude uses to decide when a rule is relevant, so the rule is never taken into account.
questoes.explicacao: Path-scoped rules load only when the file being worked on matches the `paths` glob. `migrations/*.py` matches a migrations folder at the project root, but these apps keep migrations in nested folders; a pattern such as `**/migrations/*.py` matches them wherever they are.
feedbacks: Files in `.claude/rules/` are discovered automatically; @import pulls specific files into a CLAUDE.md and is not required for rules to load. The other rules in the same folder work without it.
Phrasing can affect compliance, but here the conventions are ignored entirely while sibling rules work; that points to the rule not being loaded, not to how it is worded.
Correct. The `paths` glob determines activation, and it must match the nested app folders.
A description is how skills are chosen for on-demand use; path-scoped rules are activated by their `paths` globs, as the working sibling rules show.

questoes.pergunta: At Northgate Media, a developer asks Claude Code for a function that converts wire-agency datelines into house style. Her prompt explains the rule in a paragraph: city in capitals, state abbreviated in house style unless the city is widely known, agency name removed, date kept only for features. Over four iterations, the output changes each time: the agency name sometimes stays, and well-known cities are sometimes abbreviated. She keeps rewording the paragraph. What is the flaw in her approach?
opcoes: She adds rules across several turns instead of one message, so Claude loses earlier requirements; every rule should be restated in a single message.
She should have Claude write a test suite first and then share the failures, since prose rules cannot be checked until tests define them.
She keeps refining a prose description that is read inconsistently, when two or three concrete input-to-output dateline examples would settle it.
The transformation is too complex for one function; she should have Claude write one function per rule and compose them in a pipeline.
questoes.explicacao: When a prose description of a transformation is interpreted differently on each attempt, rewording it rarely helps. Two or three concrete input/output examples (a news dateline, a feature dateline, a well-known city) show the expected transformation directly and remove the ambiguity.
feedbacks: Sending interacting requirements together is good practice, but she already restates the whole paragraph each time; the problem is that the paragraph itself is ambiguous.
Test-driven iteration is valuable, but tests that Claude writes from the same ambiguous paragraph will encode the same misreadings. The missing ingredient is concrete expected outputs.
Correct. Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate a transformation when prose is interpreted inconsistently.
Splitting the code does not settle what the rules mean; each small function would still be written from the same ambiguous description.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Tallyway, a payments startup that runs card acquiring, merchant payouts, and a double-entry ledger, is building an internal developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar repositories, understand the legacy settlement batch service, generate boilerplate for new payment-method adapters, and automate repetitive tasks; it uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers for code search, the incident tracker, and a read-only ledger database. To answer "which services consume the `payout.settled` event?", the coordinator sends three subagents to different repository groups. In run 1, one subagent's code-search call timed out and it returned `{"status": "error", "message": "search failed"}`; the coordinator re-ran all three subagents. In run 2, the same timeout produced `{"failure_type": "timeout", "attempted": "payout.settled in ledger-* (7 of 12 repos searched)", "partial_results": [...], "alternatives": ["retry the 5 remaining repos"]}`, and the coordinator re-dispatched only those 5 repos. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The two outcomes reflect different retry policies in the coordinator; the subagent's error format is useful for logs but does not change recovery.
The run-2 payload let the coordinator retry only the unsearched repos and keep the partial results; the run-1 message left only a full re-run.
The subagent in run 1 should have retried internally until the search succeeded, so that the coordinator never has to handle such errors.
In both runs the subagent should have returned its partial results as a success, so the coordinator could proceed without any error handling.
questoes.explicacao: Structured error context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives) gives the coordinator what it needs to choose a targeted recovery. With only "search failed", the coordinator cannot know what succeeded, so re-running everything is its only safe option. The same timeout led to very different costs purely because of what the error carried.
feedbacks: The coordinator's logic was the same in both runs; what differed was the information it received. Recovery decisions can only be as precise as the error context allows.
Correct. Structured error context enables intelligent recovery decisions by the coordinator.
Local retries for transient failures are good practice, but retrying "until it succeeds" can stall the task, and errors that cannot be resolved locally must still reach the coordinator with context.
Reporting partial results as a success hides that 5 repos were never searched, so the answer would look complete when it is not; that is silent error suppression.

questoes.pergunta: Tallyway engineers also use Claude Code directly, alongside the developer productivity agent. After a migration went badly, the platform lead proposed that every task, including small ones, must start in plan mode. Today's ticket: in `validate_iban()`, reject IBANs whose country code is lowercase; the function, the failing input, and the expected error message are all known, and the change is confined to one file. How should you evaluate the proposal for this ticket?
opcoes: Apply it: plan mode is the safer default for payment code, and an extra planning step costs little compared with a regression in IBAN validation.
Apply it, but ask for a one-paragraph plan without exploration, so that the overhead stays small while the team policy is still respected.
Use direct execution here: it is a single, well-scoped change in one function with known expected behavior, so planning adds nothing useful.
Use direct execution only after the Explore subagent has mapped every caller of `validate_iban()`, so that hidden dependencies are ruled out.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode is designed for complex work: large-scale or multi-file changes, architectural decisions, several valid approaches. Adding a single validation check to one function with known inputs and outputs is the textbook case for direct execution. Applying plan mode to everything adds overhead without reducing risk where the scope is already clear.
feedbacks: Caution is understandable in payments, but the risk here is not unclear scope or design; it is a one-line rule with a known test case. Plan mode adds steps without making this change safer.
A token plan satisfies the policy on paper but still adds a step with no value; the right evaluation is that the policy does not fit well-scoped changes.
Correct. Direct execution fits simple, well-scoped changes such as one validation check in one function.
Mapping callers would matter if the function's contract changed, but rejecting malformed IBANs inside it is a well-scoped change; a full discovery phase is disproportionate.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, engineers can apply schema migrations to the staging ledger database through two MCP tools: `run_migration_dry_run` and `apply_migration`. The system prompt says to always run a dry run first and confirm there are no destructive changes. Logs show that 3 of the last 200 migrations were applied without a dry run, each time after an engineer wrote something like "it's tiny, just apply it". Engineers must keep being able to apply migrations through the agent. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Strengthen the system prompt with a firm rule and an example in which the agent refuses to skip the dry run even when an engineer insists.
Remove `apply_migration` from the agent and have engineers apply migrations by hand after reading the agent's dry-run output.
Add a PostToolUse hook that inspects each applied migration and alerts the on-call engineer whenever no dry run preceded it.
Add a programmatic gate that rejects `apply_migration` unless a successful dry run for the same migration ID was recorded in the session.
questoes.explicacao: When one step must always happen before another, prompt instructions leave a non-zero failure rate, and here users explicitly push the agent to skip it. A programmatic prerequisite that blocks the downstream call until the dry run has succeeded makes the ordering deterministic while keeping the capability available.
feedbacks: Better prompts and examples may lower the rate, but compliance stays probabilistic, and the failures happen exactly when an engineer pressures the agent.
This guarantees the order by removing the capability, which breaks the requirement that engineers keep applying migrations through the agent.
A PostToolUse hook runs after the migration has been applied; it detects the violation instead of preventing it.
Correct. A programmatic prerequisite blocks the downstream call until the required step has completed.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, an engineer has spent two hours in one interactive session understanding the legacy settlement batch service. The context is now about 85% full, mostly with long Grep outputs and full reads of generated DAO classes, and the agent warns that space is running low. The conclusions so far are still valid, the code has not changed, and she wants to keep investigating along the same line. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Run /compact so that the verbose discovery output is replaced by a summary of the session, then continue the investigation from there.
Start a brand-new session with no prior context and repeat the key searches, so that the context holds only fresh and relevant output.
Fork the session and continue in the fork, so that the original context is preserved while the fork explores the remaining questions.
Tell the agent to stop using Grep and to read only files she names, so that the remaining context fills more slowly from now on.
questoes.explicacao: /compact reduces context usage in long exploration sessions by replacing the accumulated history, here dominated by verbose discovery output, with a summary. Since the conclusions are still valid and the code has not changed, compacting and continuing is cheaper than starting over.
feedbacks: Correct. /compact is the tool for reclaiming context filled with verbose discovery output during an extended exploration.
A fresh session discards valid work and forces the searches to be repeated; starting fresh pays off when prior results are stale, which is not the case here.
A fork starts with the same full context, so it would be just as close to the limit; forking is for divergent explorations, not for freeing space.
This slows growth at the cost of the agent's ability to explore, shifts navigation to the engineer, and leaves the 85% already used untouched.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, one repetitive task is upgrading library versions across repositories. When an upgrade breaks something the agent cannot fix, it hands the work to the owning team through a ticket in the incident tracker. The owning engineers never see the agent's session. A recent handoff for the card-tokenization repository cost the owners half a day reconstructing what had happened. Which handoff design is best?
opcoes: Attach the full session transcript to the ticket, since only the complete record preserves every detail the owning engineer might need.
Post a summary listing repo and module, failing test and error, suspected root cause, what was attempted, and the recommended next step.
Post a short note with the agent's session ID, so that the owning engineer can resume that session and ask the agent questions directly.
Post the final error output and the diff the agent produced, so that the owning engineer can reproduce the failure and investigate it.
questoes.explicacao: The people receiving the handoff lack the conversation, so the handoff must be self-contained and quick to act on. A structured summary with identifiers, the observed failure, the suspected root cause, what was already tried, and a recommended action lets the owner continue without re-investigating.
feedbacks: Completeness is not usability: a transcript of tens of thousands of tokens forces the owner to dig for the same facts a summary would state up front.
Correct. A structured handoff summary gives humans without the transcript what they need to act.
The owners do not work in the agent's session, and resuming it would still require them to question the agent to reconstruct what happened.
The error and diff help reproduce the failure, but they omit the agent's diagnosis and what it already tried, so the owner repeats that work.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, an architecture-review feature analyzes the payout reconciliation module (about 40 tool calls) and then writes two alternative migration plans: one moving to event sourcing, one keeping the batch job with idempotency keys. Today the feature runs the full analysis twice, once per plan; this doubles the cost, and the two analyses sometimes disagree on basic facts (one counts 14 writers to the ledger table, the other 12). Both plans must rest on one identical analysis. What should change?
opcoes: Generate both plans one after the other in the same session, so that the second plan reuses everything learned while writing the first one.
Cache the tool results of the first analysis and replay them in the second run, so that both runs see the same file contents and outputs.
Save the first run's answer as a structured summary and pass it to two fresh sessions, so that each plan starts from the same conclusions.
Run the analysis once, then use fork_session to create two branches, one per plan, each continuing from that shared analysis baseline.
questoes.explicacao: Fork-based session management exists for exactly this: exploring divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline. Running the analysis once and forking guarantees that both plans rest on the same facts and halves the analysis cost, while each branch develops its plan independently.
feedbacks: One analysis is good, but writing the second plan in the same session means it is shaped by the first plan's reasoning; the alternatives are no longer independent.
Replaying tool outputs makes the inputs identical, but the model still reasons over them again, so the runs can still reach different conclusions, at the same doubled cost.
A shared written answer gives a common starting point, but it is a lossy summary; each plan loses the detailed tool results behind the conclusions.
Correct. fork_session creates independent branches from one shared baseline.

questoes.pergunta: Tallyway engineers also use Claude Code directly. A staff engineer notices that in her sessions on the `payouts` repo, Claude always represents amounts with the `Money` value type in minor units, but a teammate pairing on his own laptop, on the same branch, gets code with plain `decimal` amounts. She says she "added the money rule to CLAUDE.md months ago", yet `git log` shows no change to any CLAUDE.md in the repository that mentions money. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The teammate's Claude Code version is older and does not load CLAUDE.md files from the project root, so none of the project rules reach him.
She put the rule in her user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which applies only to her own sessions and is not shared through version control.
CLAUDE.md is read only when a repository is first cloned, and the teammate cloned `payouts` before the money rule was added to the file.
The rule is phrased as a preference, and Claude applies preference-style instructions inconsistently across different users and sessions.
questoes.explicacao: User-level instructions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` apply only to that user and are not committed, so teammates never receive them. The absence of any commit confirms the rule never reached the repository; it should be moved to the project CLAUDE.md.
feedbacks: If project CLAUDE.md files were not loading, other project conventions would fail too; and the git history shows there is no project-level money rule to load anyway.
Correct. User-level CLAUDE.md is personal and is not shared with teammates through version control.
CLAUDE.md files are loaded at session start, not only at clone time; and the history shows no committed money rule for either of them to read.
Wording can affect consistency, but she gets the behavior every time while he never does; that pattern points to which files each session loads.

questoes.pergunta: For a lightweight CLI version of Tallyway's developer productivity agent, an engineer wrote the loop directly against the Messages API: `messages = [task]`; on each iteration, call the API; if `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, run the tool, then set `messages = [task, {"role": "user", "content": result_text}]`; otherwise stop. The agent keeps running the same Grep for `SettlementWindow`, rediscovers the same file every iteration, and never reaches the second step of the task. What is the flaw?
opcoes: The loop should check whether the response contains assistant text before continuing, since a text block signals that the agent considers the task done.
Each iteration rebuilds the history without the assistant's tool_use turn or earlier results; it should append them, plus a tool_result, every time.
The tool output should be summarized before it is sent back, since passing raw Grep output makes the model repeat the same search to verify it.
The loop lacks an iteration cap of about 10, so the model gets no signal that it is repeating itself and that it should change its approach.
questoes.explicacao: Tool results must be appended to the conversation history, together with the assistant turn that requested them, so the model can reason about what it already did and decide the next action. Rebuilding the message list from scratch erases the previous steps, so the model starts over every time.
feedbacks: Checking for assistant text as a completion signal is an anti-pattern; continuation should depend on stop_reason, and the bug here is the lost history.
Correct. The history must accumulate: the assistant's tool_use turn, followed by a user turn with the matching tool_result.
Trimming verbose output can help the context, but the model is not repeating the search to verify it; it repeats because it has no record of having searched.
A cap would stop the loop but not fix it; iteration caps are a backstop, and the model would still lose its progress on every turn.

questoes.pergunta: Tallyway's developer productivity agent combines data from three MCP servers: the incident tracker returns times as Unix epoch seconds, the deploy-log server returns ISO 8601 strings with local offsets, and the ledger database server returns payout status as numeric codes (2 = settled, 5 = reversed). None of the servers accepts a format parameter. When engineers ask what was deployed before a payout incident, about 1 in 8 answers orders events wrongly or reports "status 5" without explaining it. Which two changes best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts every timestamp returned by these tools to ISO 8601 UTC before the agent sees the result.
Ask the three server owners to adopt one common format, and pause the feature until all of them have shipped the change.
Add a PostToolUse hook on the ledger tools that maps numeric status codes to labels such as "settled" and "reversed".
Describe each server's timestamp format and the status-code table in the system prompt, so that the agent converts the values as it reasons.
Add a PreToolUse hook that appends "return ISO 8601 times and status labels" to each tool call, so that the servers reply uniformly.
questoes.explicacao: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results before the model processes them, so heterogeneous formats can be normalized in code: one timestamp format and readable status labels. The model then reasons over consistent data instead of converting values itself, which it does unreliably.
feedbacks: Correct. A PostToolUse hook normalizes the timestamps before the agent processes them.
A shared format would be ideal in the long term, but it depends on other teams and blocks the feature; normalization can be done on the agent side now.
Correct. A PostToolUse hook can translate numeric status codes into meaningful labels before they reach the model.
Prompt guidance makes conversion likely but not guaranteed; with three formats and a code table, the model still slips, as the 1-in-8 error rate shows.
PreToolUse hooks intercept outgoing calls, but the servers accept no format parameter, so extra text in the arguments changes nothing; results still arrive in three formats.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, a "dependency map" feature helps new engineers understand the settlement system: the coordinator sends one subagent per repository and then synthesizes a report. In this week's run, the subagent for the `fx-rates` repository got a permission error from the code-search server, so that repository could not be analyzed; the other 11 were analyzed fully. A reviewer proposes that the report should fail whenever any repository is unavailable, "so nobody relies on an incomplete map". How should you evaluate the proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: an incomplete map is worse than none in payments code, so the report should be produced only when every repository has been analyzed.
Reject it: publish with coverage annotations marking well-supported sections and stating that `fx-rates` dependencies could not be analyzed.
Reject it: publish the report and leave `fx-rates` out entirely, so that the map contains only verified findings and no uncertain sections.
Accept a variant: retry the `fx-rates` analysis until access succeeds and only then generate the report, so that it is complete when read.
questoes.explicacao: A single failure should not discard eleven valid analyses, and it should not be hidden either. Coverage annotations let the synthesis state which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps because a source was unavailable, so readers can rely on the map while knowing its limits.
feedbacks: Terminating the whole workflow on a single failure is an anti-pattern: eleven valid analyses are thrown away when the gap could simply be stated.
Correct. Coverage annotations distinguish well-supported findings from gaps caused by unavailable sources.
Omitting `fx-rates` silently makes the map look complete; readers would wrongly conclude that nothing depends on it.
A permission error is not transient, so retrying will not fix it; the report would be delayed indefinitely.

questoes.pergunta: Tallyway's developer productivity agent uses a coordinator with three subagents: `repo_explorer`, `test_writer`, and `docs_writer`. To save time, a developer let `test_writer` call `repo_explorer` directly and let `docs_writer` read `test_writer`'s scratch output. Since then, failures in `repo_explorer` go unnoticed by the coordinator, traces show duplicated exploration, and nobody can tell where a wrong claim in the generated docs came from. Which two statements describe the architecture the team should restore? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Direct calls between subagents are acceptable as long as each call is logged, so that the traces show which agent asked which one for what.
Subagents should share one structured memory store that each reads and writes, so that findings move between them without the coordinator.
All communication between subagents should flow through the coordinator, which decides what each one receives and keeps a record of it.
Errors a subagent cannot resolve should go to the coordinator, which decides whether to retry, reroute the work, or continue with partial results.
Each subagent should absorb its own failures and report to the coordinator only when its whole task is done, so the coordinator stays simple.
questoes.explicacao: In a hub-and-spoke architecture, the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing. Routing everything through it restores observability (where each claim came from), consistent error handling (failures are seen and acted on), and controlled information flow (no duplicated exploration).
feedbacks: Logging improves traces, but the coordinator still neither controls nor sees the information flow, so duplicated work and unhandled failures remain.
A shared store is still communication that bypasses the coordinator; it removes control over what each agent sees and makes the origin of claims hard to trace.
Correct. In hub-and-spoke, the coordinator routes all inter-subagent communication.
Correct. The coordinator handles errors that subagents cannot resolve and decides how to recover.
Local recovery for transient failures is good, but holding unresolved failures until the end leaves the coordinator blind to them, which is the problem already observed.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, an engineer asked the agent to "map every place where card numbers (PAN) are handled". The coordinator spawned four parallel subagents with that same instruction. Traces show that each one searched the same 6 repositories, 70% of their findings were duplicates, and the task cost about four times as much as a single search. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Have the coordinator give each subagent a distinct slice of the scope, such as separate repositories or source types (code, configs, log schemas).
Add a deduplication step after the subagents finish that merges identical findings, so that the final map lists each location only once.
Use a single subagent that searches all repositories in sequence, so that no two agents can examine the same file during the task.
Have each subagent read the others' findings from a shared file before searching, so that each one skips what was already covered.
questoes.explicacao: Parallel subagents add value only when they cover different ground. Partitioning the scope (distinct repositories, subtopics, or source types per subagent) removes duplicated work at the source while keeping the parallel speed-up.
feedbacks: Correct. Partition the scope across subagents to minimize duplication.
Deduplication cleans the output but still pays for four overlapping searches; it treats the symptom rather than the assignment that caused it.
This removes duplication by giving up parallelism, so the task takes longer when partitioning would give both benefits.
Coordinating through a shared file bypasses the coordinator and races: subagents running in parallel will often read the file before the others have written to it.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, the loop that generates boilerplate for new payment-method adapters needs a termination rule. Engineer 1 stops the loop when the response text contains "Done" or "All files generated"; in 6% of runs it stopped after the model wrote "Done with the DTOs, now the mapper...". Engineer 2 stops after 15 iterations; large adapters were cut off half-finished. Which termination design should the team adopt?
opcoes: Combine both rules: stop when a completion phrase appears or when 15 iterations are reached, whichever comes first, so each covers the other's gaps.
Stop as soon as a response includes an assistant text block, since the model writes a text summary only after it has finished the whole task.
Raise the cap to 50 iterations and keep the phrase check, so that large adapters can finish while short tasks still end once they are done.
Continue while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop when it is "end_turn", keeping a generous iteration cap only as a safety backstop.
questoes.explicacao: The model signals its intent through stop_reason: "tool_use" means it is requesting a tool, so the loop executes it and continues; "end_turn" means it has finished. Parsing natural-language phrases, relying on the presence of text, or using an iteration cap as the primary stop are all unreliable; a cap is acceptable only as a backstop.
feedbacks: Combining two unreliable signals keeps both failure modes: premature stops on phrases and truncation at the cap.
Assistant text often accompanies tool calls (the model explains what it will do next), so the presence of text is not a completion indicator.
A higher cap reduces truncation but is still arbitrary, and the phrase check still ends runs early whenever the model mentions its progress.
Correct. Loop control should follow stop_reason: continue on "tool_use", end on "end_turn".

questoes.pergunta: Tallyway's developer productivity agent can call `create_payout_adjustment` on an internal MCP server to fix test fixtures in staging, but the same tool accepts `env: "production"`. Policy says that production adjustments above $500 need approval from finance operations through a ticket. An audit found two production adjustments of $1,200 that the agent made after engineers asked for them. Engineers still need the tool for staging work. Which two changes best enforce the policy? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks `create_payout_adjustment` calls with env production and an amount above $500 before they run.
Have blocked calls return a message telling the agent to open a finance approval ticket through the incident tracker instead.
Add a PostToolUse hook that reverses any production adjustment above $500 right after it runs and notifies finance operations.
State the $500 production limit in the system prompt and in the tool description, so that the agent asks for finance approval before calling it.
Remove `create_payout_adjustment` from the agent's toolset, so that every adjustment, in any environment, goes through finance.
questoes.explicacao: A hook that intercepts outgoing tool calls enforces a business rule deterministically: the violating call never executes, whatever the conversation says. Redirecting the blocked action to the approved workflow (an approval ticket) lets the agent still help the engineer instead of simply failing.
feedbacks: Correct. Intercepting the outgoing call blocks policy-violating actions before they execute.
Correct. Blocking is paired with a redirect to the alternative workflow, so the agent can still complete the request properly.
Reversing after execution means the money has already moved and the ledger records an adjustment plus a reversal; for financial actions, prevention beats cleanup.
Prompt and description rules are probabilistic, and these violations happened precisely when engineers asked for the adjustment.
This enforces the rule by removing a capability engineers need for staging, when only one combination of environment and amount is restricted.

questoes.pergunta: In Tallyway's developer productivity agent, the coordinator's prompt to the `legacy_analyzer` subagent reads: "1. Glob for *.java under settlement/. 2. Read SettlementJob.java. 3. Grep for BatchWriter. 4. Summarize the settlement logic." This works for the older repositories. For the newer `payouts-v2` repository, written in Kotlin with no `SettlementJob` class, the subagent returns "SettlementJob.java not found; no settlement logic present", although the logic exists in `PayoutCloser.kt`. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The subagent lacks a Grep configuration for Kotlin files, so its searches could not match the class names used in the newer repository.
The subagent's context was too small to hold the Kotlin sources, so it stopped before reaching the files that contain the settlement logic.
The subagent's model handles Kotlin less well than Java, so it failed to recognize settlement code that a stronger model would have found.
The coordinator prescribed a fixed procedure instead of stating the goal and what a complete answer must contain, so the subagent could not adapt.
questoes.explicacao: Step-by-step procedural instructions work only when the situation matches the procedure's assumptions. Stating the research goal (for example, "identify where settlement batches are closed and written") and quality criteria lets the subagent adapt its search to a Kotlin codebase with different names.
feedbacks: Grep searches any text file regardless of language; nothing in the trace suggests a failed search, because the procedure never searched for the right things.
The subagent followed the steps and stopped at a missing file; the failure is in what it was told to do, not in how much it could hold.
The subagent never looked beyond the prescribed Java file, so the model's Kotlin ability was never actually tested.
Correct. Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, so that subagents can adapt.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Furrow Labs, an agritech company that sells soil-sensor irrigation systems, has integrated Claude Code into the CI/CD pipeline of its Python sensor-ingestion platform and its TypeScript farm-management app. The pipeline runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and posts feedback on pull requests, and the team must design prompts that produce actionable feedback with few false positives. Reviews often meet an ambiguous pattern: calling `to_mm()` twice on irrigation volumes is a bug when the value is already metric, but correct when two different readings are being converted. The team added 12 few-shot examples to the review prompt, each a clear double-conversion bug labeled only "Issue: double conversion". Since then, the review flags every repeated call to `to_mm()`, including the correct ones. What is the flaw in these examples?
opcoes: Twelve examples are more than the model can use well, so it falls back on the simplest rule they share: flag any repeated call to `to_mm()`.
The examples belong in the project CLAUDE.md rather than in the prompt, so that the review job loads them as project context instead.
They show only clear-cut bugs with bare labels; a few ambiguous cases with reasoning on why each was flagged or accepted are needed.
Few-shot examples cannot teach judgment on ambiguous cases, so a rule listing every legitimate use of `to_mm()` should replace them.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples work best for ambiguous cases when they show the reasoning behind each decision, including cases where the plausible alternative (flagging) was rejected. Examples that show one outcome with a bare label teach the surface pattern "repeated `to_mm()` = bug". Two to four targeted examples, covering both sides and explaining why, let the model generalize the judgment.
feedbacks: The number is not the issue; the model learned the pattern the examples actually share, which is that every repeated call is a bug.
Moving the examples changes where they are loaded, not what they teach; they would still show only one side of the ambiguity.
Correct. Targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous cases should show the reasoning for choosing one action over plausible alternatives.
Few-shot examples are effective for ambiguous judgment when they show reasoning; an exhaustive list of legitimate uses cannot keep up with new code.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, a step calls the Claude API to turn raw job logs into structured records. The log type is not known in advance, so the request offers three tools with different schemas: `report_test_failure`, `report_lint_issue`, and `report_build_error`. With `tool_choice` set to `{"type": "auto"}`, about 4% of responses are prose ("The build failed because...") and the parser drops them. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The prose replies happen because the three schemas overlap; merging them into one generic schema would make the model call a tool on every log.
Forcing `{"type": "tool", "name": "report_test_failure"}` would guarantee a tool call and still let the model choose the schema that fits.
With "auto" the model may answer in text; "any" requires it to call one of the tools while still letting it choose the schema that fits.
With "auto" the model must call a tool whenever tools are provided, so the prose replies point to a parsing bug rather than to configuration.
questoes.explicacao: "auto" lets the model decide whether to use a tool at all, so it sometimes replies in text. "any" guarantees a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to the model, which is exactly what is needed when several extraction schemas exist and the input type is unknown. Forcing one named tool would remove that choice.
feedbacks: Merging schemas weakens the structure and does not change the setting that allows text replies; with "auto", a single tool can also be skipped.
Forced selection guarantees a call to that one tool, so every log would be reported as a test failure, including lint and build errors.
Correct. "any" forces a tool call but lets the model choose which tool fits the input.
"auto" is precisely the mode in which the model may return text instead of calling a tool; the parser is behaving correctly.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, every pull request goes through a fixed chain: a security pass, a pass on validation of incoming sensor data, a test-coverage pass, and a summary. Results are consistent and reviewers trust them. A separate nightly job that investigates why yield-prediction accuracy dropped in some regions improved a lot after switching to an agent that plans its own next steps. A teammate proposes replacing the PR chain with the same self-planning agent. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: self-planning generalizes better, so the PR review will also find problems that the three fixed passes were never designed to look for.
Keep the fixed chain for PR reviews, whose aspects are known in advance, and keep adaptive decomposition for open-ended work like the accuracy drop.
Adopt it, but log the steps the agent chooses on every PR, so that reviewers can audit whether each plan still covered the three required aspects.
Keep the fixed chain for PRs and move the nightly investigation onto fixed passes as well, so that both jobs are equally deterministic and auditable.
questoes.explicacao: Prompt chaining suits predictable, multi-aspect reviews: the aspects are known, and a fixed sequence gives consistent coverage on every PR. Dynamic decomposition suits open-ended investigations, where the next subtask depends on what was found. Each job is already using the pattern that fits it.
feedbacks: Adaptive decomposition helped the investigation because its path was unknown; on PR reviews, it makes coverage of the required aspects vary from run to run.
Correct. Use prompt chaining for predictable multi-aspect reviews and dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation.
Logging lets you detect when a dynamic plan skipped an aspect, but only after the fact; the fixed chain guarantees that coverage up front.
Fixed passes would make the investigation predictable but blind: in an investigation, the next step should depend on what the previous one found.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, a pull request changes 26 files in the sensor-ingestion service, including a change to the `Reading` dataclass and to its consumers. The single-pass review gives detailed comments on the first files in the diff, one-line remarks on the rest, and misses that two consumers still read the removed field `soil_temp_f`. Which two changes to the review structure best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Sort the files so the most-changed ones come first in the single pass, so that the model gives its closest attention to the riskiest code.
Add an instruction to the single-pass prompt to give every file the same depth of analysis, so that later files are no longer skimmed.
Add a separate integration pass that examines cross-file data flow, such as the `Reading` change and every consumer of its fields.
Review only files with more than 50 changed lines, so that the model's attention is concentrated on the changes most likely to hold bugs.
Review each file in its own focused pass for local issues, so that every file receives the same depth regardless of its position.
questoes.explicacao: The symptoms are attention dilution: depth drops as more files share one pass, and cross-file issues get lost. Splitting the review into per-file passes for local issues plus a separate cross-file integration pass gives each file consistent attention and gives data-flow problems, like a removed field that is still read elsewhere, a pass of their own.
feedbacks: Reordering changes which files get the attention but keeps the dilution; files with few changes can hold bugs too, and cross-file flow is still unexamined.
An instruction cannot add attention the single pass lacks; the drop in depth comes from the structure, not from a lack of intent.
Correct. A separate integration pass catches cross-file data-flow problems that per-file passes cannot see.
Skipping small changes hides real bugs (a one-line field removal can break consumers) and does nothing for cross-file issues.
Correct. Per-file passes give each file focused, consistent analysis.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, the automated review posts findings in five categories. Over two months, 78% of "performance" findings were dismissed, while "security" and "sensor data validation" findings were accepted about 85% of the time. Developers now skim past all bot comments, and last week two valid security findings were ignored until a manual audit caught them. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add "only report performance issues you are highly confident about" to the prompt, so that the model filters out its weakest findings.
Post all findings as one collapsed summary comment instead of inline, so that developers are not overwhelmed by inline bot noise.
Have an independent second Claude instance confirm every performance finding before posting, so that only agreed findings appear.
Switch off that one noisy category until its criteria are rewritten, and keep the high-acceptance categories posting as before.
questoes.explicacao: A high false-positive category erodes trust in every category, including the accurate ones. Temporarily disabling the noisy category restores trust right away while its prompt and criteria are improved, and the high-precision categories keep delivering value in the meantime.
feedbacks: Confidence-based filtering instructions do not improve precision the way specific criteria do; the model's sense of "confident" is the same one producing the noise.
Collapsing everything hides the accurate security findings along with the noise, so the trust problem gets worse, not better.
An independent reviewer can help later, but it adds cost and latency and may still agree with a vague category; disabling the category restores trust at once.
Correct. Temporarily disabling high false-positive categories restores developer trust while the prompts are improved.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, the tech lead's local reviews with Claude Code follow the team's review criteria: flag unchecked unit conversions, ignore formatting. In CI, where `claude -p` runs on a fresh runner, the reviews ignore those criteria. The criteria live in the lead's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. One engineer proposes moving them into the repository's CLAUDE.md; another proposes having the CI job copy the lead's file into the runner's home directory before each run. Which is the better choice?
opcoes: Move the criteria into the project CLAUDE.md in the repository, so that CI and every developer load the same version-controlled instructions.
Copy the lead's user-level file onto the runner before each job, so that CI matches the lead's local behavior without touching the repository.
Pass the criteria inline in the CI job's `-p` prompt, so that the review instructions live in the pipeline definition rather than in a file.
Keep the criteria in the lead's file and run `/memory` at the start of each CI job, so that missing instructions make the job fail early.
questoes.explicacao: The criteria never reached CI because they are in user-level configuration, which applies only to the lead. Moving them to the project CLAUDE.md puts them under version control, so CI and every developer load the same instructions, and changes are reviewed like code.
feedbacks: Correct. Team instructions belong in the project-level CLAUDE.md, which CI and every clone load.
This makes CI depend on one person's personal file, which can change without review, and it still leaves other developers without the criteria.
Inline prompts work for CI, but local reviews by other developers still lack the criteria, and two copies of the same rules will drift apart.
/memory is an interactive way to see which memory files are loaded; it is a diagnostic, and the instructions would still be missing from CI.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, after an earlier fix, large pull requests are reviewed one file at a time, and local findings have become consistent. But last month two contract breaks reached production: a producer renamed a payload field from `moisture_pct` to `moisture_ratio` while a consumer in another file kept reading the old name, and each file looked fine on its own. The team needs reviews to catch this class of issue. What should change?
opcoes: Give each per-file pass the full diff of the pull request as extra context, so that each file is reviewed knowing every other change in the PR.
Add a separate integration pass after the per-file passes that examines data flow across files, such as the producers and consumers of fields.
Add explicit few-shot examples of contract breaks to the per-file prompt, so that each per-file pass learns to spot renamed fields and stale reads.
Review each file together with its two most closely related files, chosen from the import graph, so that each pass sees its immediate neighbors.
questoes.explicacao: Per-file passes find local issues consistently but, by design, cannot see how a change in one file affects another. A separate integration pass focused on cross-file data flow (producers, consumers, shared contracts) catches those issues without bringing back the attention dilution of a single large pass.
feedbacks: Loading the entire diff into each pass reintroduces the dilution the per-file split removed, and each pass is still focused on its own file.
Correct. Per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow.
Better examples cannot help a pass that never sees the other file; the stale read is visible only when both files are examined together.
Neighbor windows catch some direct imports, but data contracts often cross through queues or serialized payloads that an import graph does not show.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, a nightly job asks Claude Code to generate unit tests for the modules changed that day in `irrigation/scheduler/`. Reviewers reject about 60% of the generated tests because they repeat scenarios already covered in `tests/scheduler/test_windows.py`, such as "frost delay skips the watering window", under different names. The job's prompt includes the diff of the changed modules, and the project CLAUDE.md documents the testing standards. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The testing standards in CLAUDE.md are too general, so Claude writes generic scheduling tests that happen to overlap with the existing ones.
The job runs as a nightly batch, so the tests for each module are generated in isolation and are never compared with one another.
Claude is not given the existing test files for these modules, so it cannot tell which scenarios the suite already covers.
The diff alone shows too little of each module's behavior, so Claude falls back on the most common scenarios for scheduling code.
questoes.explicacao: To avoid duplicating coverage, test generation needs to see what the suite already tests. Providing the existing test files for the changed modules lets Claude target uncovered behavior instead of rediscovering scenarios like the frost delay.
feedbacks: Clearer standards improve quality, but no standard tells Claude which scenarios already exist; the duplicates match specific existing tests, not generic ones.
How the generation runs are grouped is not the problem; the duplicates are of the existing suite, which the job never shows Claude.
Correct. Providing the existing test files in context prevents test generation from duplicating covered scenarios.
More module context could improve the tests, but the specific failure is repeating existing tests, which only the existing test files can prevent.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, one step calls the Claude API directly with two tools: `post_inline_comment` and `approve_without_comments`. To make sure every response is structured, the engineer set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "post_inline_comment"}`. Since then, PRs with no real problems (about 30% of them) get at least one low-value comment such as "consider renaming this variable", and `approve_without_comments` is never called. What is the flaw?
opcoes: The `approve_without_comments` description is too short, so the model does not recognize when a pull request is clean enough to approve.
The prompt lacks explicit criteria for what to report, so the model pads clean pull requests with style comments to appear thorough.
Forcing one tool means the model must call `post_inline_comment` every time; "any" would still require a tool call but allow approving.
The value should be "auto", because only "auto" lets the model choose among tools, while "any" always calls the first tool listed.
questoes.explicacao: Forced tool selection makes the model call that specific tool, so on a clean PR it has to invent a comment. "any" still guarantees a tool call (structured output) but lets the model choose between commenting and approving, while "auto" would also allow a plain-text reply.
feedbacks: Better descriptions help selection only when the model is allowed to choose; with forced selection, approval can never be selected.
