Explicit criteria matter for precision, but no criteria can produce an approval when the configuration requires a comment on every call.
Correct. Forced selection requires that named tool; "any" requires some tool and leaves the choice to the model.
"any" does not pick the first tool; it requires a call to one of the tools, chosen by the model. "auto" would also allow text replies, losing the guarantee.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, test files live next to the code in about 40 packages (`*/tests/test_*.py`), and generated tests must use the `reading_factory` fixture instead of hard-coded timestamps. The team wrote these conventions in `ingestion/CLAUDE.md`. Tests generated for `ingestion/` follow them; tests generated for `weather/` and `yield/` do not. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: A directory-level CLAUDE.md applies to the whole repository once any file in its directory has been read, so the job never read files in `ingestion/`.
Each package's CLAUDE.md must @import `ingestion/CLAUDE.md`, since importing is the only way to apply one set of conventions in several directories.
A directory CLAUDE.md applies only within its directory; a `.claude/rules/` file with a glob like `**/tests/test_*.py` applies wherever tests live.
Test conventions belong in a skill, because skills load automatically whenever Claude edits a file whose name matches the name of the skill.
questoes.explicacao: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are bound to their directory, so conventions placed there do not reach test files in other packages. Path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/` use glob patterns that match files by type regardless of location, which is the right tool when a convention spans many directories.
feedbacks: A directory CLAUDE.md does not extend to the rest of the repository; the conventions worked in `ingestion/` precisely because that is where the file lives.
@import can share a standards file between packages, but it is not the only way, and adding it to 40 package files is harder to maintain than one glob-scoped rule.
Correct. Glob-scoped rules apply to files spread across the codebase, which directory CLAUDE.md files cannot do.
Skills are invoked on demand or chosen by their description, not loaded by file-name matching; path-scoped rules are what load by file pattern.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, a pull request to the farm-management app changes 17 files. The single-pass review flagged the null handling in `parseFieldBoundary()` as a bug in `map/editor.ts` but approved identical code in `map/import.ts`. It also missed that `areaHectares` was renamed in the API response while two components still read the old name. Which two statements about this review are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Reviewing many files in a single pass dilutes attention, which can produce contradictory verdicts on identical code in different files.
Per-file passes alone would catch the `areaHectares` rename, since each component would be reviewed against its own part of the diff.
Catching the renamed field needs a separate integration pass over cross-file data flow, which per-file passes cannot see on their own.
Asking the same session to re-check its findings for consistency before posting would resolve the contradiction without changing the structure.
The opposite verdicts show that the prompt is too loose; once the review instructions are precise enough, one pass over all 17 files is reliable.
questoes.explicacao: Multi-pass review splits large reviews into per-file local passes plus cross-file integration passes. Per-file passes counter attention dilution, which causes uneven depth and contradictory findings on identical code; the integration pass catches issues that span files, such as a renamed field and its stale readers.
feedbacks: Correct. Attention dilution in large single-pass reviews causes contradictory findings.
The components' own diffs may not change at all; the stale reads become visible only when the API change and its consumers are examined together.
Correct. Cross-file issues need a dedicated integration pass.
The same session keeps its earlier reasoning and tends to confirm itself, and the missed rename would remain undetected.
Precise instructions help, but they do not remove the attention dilution of a 17-file pass; contradictory verdicts on identical code are a symptom of that dilution.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, an engineer wrote a `/triage-flaky` command that analyzes flaky tests. It lives in `~/.claude/commands/triage-flaky.md` on his laptop. Teammates on the on-call rotation get "unknown command" when they run it, and the nightly CI job that calls it fails with the same error. The team wants a single definition whose changes are reviewed in pull requests. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Move the file to `.claude/commands/triage-flaky.md` in the repository, so that it is versioned, reviewed, and available in every clone and in CI.
Ask each on-call engineer to copy the file into their own `~/.claude/commands/`, and add the same copy step to the CI runner image.
Paste the command's instructions into the project CLAUDE.md under a `/triage-flaky` heading, so that every session recognizes the command.
Turn it into a personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/triage-flaky/`, so that Claude invokes it automatically whenever flaky tests are mentioned.
questoes.explicacao: Commands in `~/.claude/commands/` are personal and exist only on that machine. Project-scoped commands in `.claude/commands/` are committed with the repository, so every clone, including the CI checkout, has the same definition, and changes go through pull requests.
feedbacks: Correct. Project-scoped commands in `.claude/commands/` are shared via version control.
Copies in personal directories drift apart and bypass review; the team asked for a single, reviewed definition.
CLAUDE.md holds instructions and context; a heading there does not define a slash command.
A skill under `~/.claude/skills/` is still personal to his machine, so teammates and CI would still not have it.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, the review labels each finding critical, major, or minor, and merges are blocked on critical. The same kind of issue, an unvalidated sensor reading flowing into the irrigation-volume calculation, was labeled critical on one PR and minor on another. The prompt says: "Use critical for serious problems, major for important ones, and minor for small ones." Which two changes would most improve consistency? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Include short code examples for each level, such as a snippet that is critical and a similar one that is only minor, to anchor them.
Classify each finding's severity three times and keep the most common label, so that random variation between runs averages out.
Define each level by explicit impact criteria, for example "critical: can produce wrong irrigation volumes or lose sensor data in production".
Have the model report a confidence score with each severity, and downgrade any critical finding below 0.8 to major before posting it.
Add a deterministic tie-break rule: when two levels seem to apply, always choose the lower one, so that borderline findings match.
questoes.explicacao: Vague severity labels let each review interpret "serious" differently. Explicit criteria for each level, tied to concrete impact, plus code examples that show what each level looks like, give the model a consistent reference, and that is what produces consistent classification.
feedbacks: Correct. Concrete code examples for each severity level anchor consistent classification.
Majority voting hides variance at triple the cost; if the definitions are vague, the most common label can still be wrong.
Correct. Explicit severity criteria remove the ambiguity of words like "serious".
Confidence thresholds filter findings but do not define what each level means; the inconsistency comes from vague definitions, not from low confidence.
A tie-break makes borderline labels predictable but systematically under-labels real critical issues, and it still does not define what "critical" means.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, the project skill `.claude/skills/gen-tests/SKILL.md` generates unit tests, both locally and in the nightly job. A senior developer wants to experiment with a version that also generates property-based tests with Hypothesis, for his own use only, without affecting teammates or CI. Which option best meets that goal?
opcoes: Edit the project skill so that the property-based steps run only when he passes a `--property` argument, keeping one definition for everyone.
Create a personal variant in `~/.claude/skills/` under a different name, such as `gen-tests-prop`, leaving the team's skill untouched.
Create a personal copy in `~/.claude/skills/gen-tests/` with the same name, so that his version replaces the team skill on his machine only.
Add the property-based instructions to his `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so that they apply whenever he invokes the project's gen-tests skill.
questoes.explicacao: Personal variants of team skills go in `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name: they are available only to that developer, and the shared skill that teammates and CI rely on stays unchanged. A distinct name also lets him run either version deliberately.
feedbacks: Editing the shared skill changes what teammates and CI run, and an experiment's instructions now ship to everyone through the repository.
Correct. Personal variants in `~/.claude/skills/` with different names avoid affecting teammates.
Reusing the name makes the two definitions collide: which one runs depends on precedence rules rather than on his choice, and he loses easy access to the team version.
User-level CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so these instructions would leak into all of his sessions; skills are the place for on-demand, task-specific workflows.

questoes.pergunta: In Furrow Labs' CI pipeline, tickets labeled `auto-fix` (such as adjusting a sensor threshold) are implemented by Claude Code in a CI job; then, in the same session, Claude writes a "risk review" comment before a human approves. Ninety-four percent of these reviews say "no significant risks identified", yet humans later find problems in about one in five of these PRs. The team wants the automated review to surface subtle issues before humans see the PR. What should change?
opcoes: Run the review in a separate Claude Code invocation that receives only the diff and the project context, not the session that wrote the code.
Keep the same session but instruct it explicitly to assume the change is wrong and look for problems, so that its review becomes adversarial.
Keep the same session and enable extended thinking for the review step, so that the model reasons longer before it judges its own change.
Have the same session write two alternative implementations and compare them with the first, so that it judges options rather than one change.
questoes.explicacao: A session that generated the code retains its reasoning and is unlikely to question its own decisions. An independent review instance, without the generator's context, evaluates the change on its merits and is more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review prompts or extended thinking.
feedbacks: Correct. An independent review instance is not anchored by the reasoning that produced the change.
An adversarial instruction does not remove the generator's context; the session still reads the change through the reasoning that justified it.
Longer reasoning in the same context tends to re-justify the same decisions; independent instances beat extended thinking for reviewing generated code.
Comparing alternatives is still self-review from the same context, and it adds cost without bringing an outside perspective.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Coursewell, an ed-tech platform that handles credit transfer between universities, is building a system that uses Claude to extract information from unstructured documents: course syllabi, student transcripts, and accreditation reports from partner universities. Outputs are validated against JSON schemas, must stay highly accurate, must handle edge cases gracefully, and feed downstream systems such as the course catalog and the credit-transfer engine. The team removed human review for extractions with confidence of 0.9 or higher after a validation run on 2,000 documents showed 96% field accuracy. Two weeks later, the credit-transfer team reports many wrong credit-hour values from scanned transcripts of quarter-system universities. Transcripts were 6% of the validation set; syllabi were 80%. What most likely explains why this was not caught before human review was removed?
opcoes: The decision relied on aggregate accuracy without checking it per document type and field, so a weak segment like transcript credit hours stayed hidden.
The 0.9 threshold was set too low; recalibrating it to 0.97 would have kept the problematic transcript extractions in the human review queue.
The schema has no field for the academic calendar system, so the model could not know when credit hours needed conversion between systems.
The validation set was too small; 2,000 documents cannot measure accuracy reliably, and a set of 10,000 documents would have exposed the issue.
questoes.explicacao: Aggregate accuracy can hide poor performance on specific document types or fields, especially when those segments are a small share of the validation set. Before automating high-confidence extractions, accuracy must be checked per document type and per field; here, transcript credit hours would have stood out.
feedbacks: Correct. Validate accuracy by document type and field segment before automating.
A higher threshold might hold back some cases, but without per-segment analysis nobody knows whether confidence is meaningful for transcripts at all.
A calendar field might improve the extraction itself, but the question is why validation did not reveal the problem; the masking came from aggregate metrics.
A bigger set with the same mix would still be dominated by syllabi; the issue is how the results were analyzed, not the sample size.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, the agent chooses between `extract_transcript_grades` and `extract_syllabus_outline`. Last month both descriptions were rewritten with input formats, examples, and boundaries, yet 31% of transcripts are still routed to `extract_syllabus_outline`, which returns empty grade data. The system prompt includes: "Whenever a document mentions a course, use extract_syllabus_outline to capture it." What is the flaw?
opcoes: The two descriptions still overlap; the tools should be merged into one `extract_course_data` tool that detects the document type internally.
The agent needs few-shot examples of transcripts and syllabi, since descriptions alone cannot separate documents that both list courses.
The agent should force `extract_transcript_grades` whenever the file name contains "transcript", so that routing no longer depends on the model.
The keyword rule in the system prompt ("mentions a course") steers selection to the syllabus tool and overrides the improved descriptions.
questoes.explicacao: Transcripts list courses too, so a keyword-sensitive system-prompt instruction associates them with the syllabus tool, overriding well-written descriptions. Reviewing the system prompt for such keyword triggers, and removing or rewording them, is what lets the improved descriptions do their job.
feedbacks: Consolidation is a heavier change and unnecessary here: the descriptions were already improved, and the routing problem comes from the system prompt.
Few-shot examples can help with ambiguous selection, but they would be fighting an explicit instruction that keeps pointing transcripts to the wrong tool.
File names are an unreliable signal (many uploads are named like "scan_0042.pdf"), and this bypasses the model instead of fixing what misleads it.
Correct. Keyword-sensitive system-prompt instructions can override well-written tool descriptions.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, the nightly re-extraction of about 30,000 archived syllabi was moved to the Message Batches API. Over three weeks, most batches finished in under two hours, but one took 19 hours, and the 8:00 catalog refresh, which waits for the batch, published stale data. Engineers disagree about what happened. Which statement is correct?
opcoes: This is within expected behavior: batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so the refresh must not assume a two-hour finish.
A 19-hour batch points to a malformed submission, since batches finish within the hour unless requests fail, so it should be resubmitted.
The batch was too large; splitting it into batches of under 1,000 requests guarantees that each one finishes within a few hours.
Batches are slow only when they are small; large batches run as fast as synchronous calls while still costing about 50% less.
questoes.explicacao: The Message Batches API offers about 50% cost savings in exchange for a processing window of up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. Fast completions are common but not promised, so any downstream schedule must tolerate the full window.
feedbacks: Correct. Batches have a processing window of up to 24 hours with no latency SLA.
A long processing time is not a sign of failure; failed requests are reported per request, and nothing guarantees completion within an hour.
Smaller batches may often finish sooner, but there is no latency guarantee for any batch size.
Batch size does not turn the batch API into a low-latency service; the trade-off is lower cost for a window of up to 24 hours.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, an extraction agent (tools: `extract_syllabus`, `extract_transcript`) feeds a catalog-matching agent (tools: `search_catalog`, `match_equivalent_course`). To save a round trip, a developer proposes giving the extraction agent the two catalog tools as well. In a one-week pilot of that change, the extraction agent replaced extracted course titles with the titles of "similar" catalog courses in 9% of documents. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: the pilot errors come from vague catalog tool descriptions, which can be rewritten while keeping the round-trip savings.
Adopt it with a prompt rule saying the extraction agent may use catalog tools only to check values, never to overwrite extracted ones.
Adopt it and give the extraction agent every tool of both agents, so that it completes every step without coordinator handoffs.
Reject it: tools outside an agent's role invite misuse, as the pilot shows; keep matching with the agent that specializes in it.
questoes.explicacao: Agents given tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them; here the extraction agent started "matching" while extracting, corrupting values that should stay faithful to the source. Keeping each agent's tools scoped to its role prevents this cross-specialization misuse.
feedbacks: Better descriptions do not change the role mismatch: once matching tools are available during extraction, the agent will use them in the wrong step.
A prompt rule makes the misuse less likely, not impossible, and the pilot's 9% shows how readily the agent reaches for these tools.
Giving one agent every tool increases decision complexity and makes cross-role misuse more likely, not less.
Correct. Restrict each agent's tools to its role to prevent cross-specialization misuse.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, accreditation reports of more than 300 pages are processed in chunks, with a running summary passed from each chunk to the next. The final output says "most programs meet credit requirements, with some deadlines approaching", although the report states "Nursing BSN: 118 of 120 required credits; corrective plan due 2027-03-01". The chunked approach must stay, because the reports do not fit in one request. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Ask the model to write a longer and more detailed running summary at each chunk, so that fewer specifics are lost as it is carried forward.
Use the largest chunks that fit in one request, so that the running summary is rewritten fewer times before the end of the report.
Extract figures, dates, and program-level requirements into a separate facts record carried alongside the summary and never re-summarized.
Add a final pass that reviews the running summary and restores any figures that seem to be missing, so that the output is complete.
questoes.explicacao: Progressive summarization condenses numbers, percentages, and dates into vague statements, and each rewrite loses more. Keeping transactional facts in a separate structured record that is passed along unchanged, outside the summarized text, preserves exact values like "118 of 120" and "2027-03-01".
feedbacks: Longer summaries delay the loss but do not stop it; every rewrite is another chance to condense exact values into generalities.
Fewer rewrites reduce the loss somewhat, but the remaining summarization steps still turn exact figures into vague statements.
Correct. Persist key facts outside the summarized history so they are not condensed.
Once a figure has been summarized away, the final pass has nothing to restore it from; it would have to guess.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, the `learning_outcomes` field must hold one outcome per item, starting with an action verb, keeping the original wording, without numbering. The prompt spends about 600 words describing these rules. Outputs still vary: some items keep their numbering, some merge two outcomes, and some are paraphrased. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add two or three examples, each a syllabus excerpt with its exact expected outcome list, including one where merged outcomes are split correctly.
Turn the formatting rules into a checklist and repeat it at both the start and the end of the prompt, so that every rule receives emphasis.
Post-process the outputs with regular expressions that strip numbering and split merged items, so that format errors are fixed downstream.
Move the extraction to a larger model, since inconsistent formatting despite detailed instructions shows the model cannot follow long prompts.
questoes.explicacao: When detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent formatting, few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistent output: they show the exact expected result instead of describing it. Including a tricky case (merged outcomes) demonstrates how to handle it.
feedbacks: Correct. Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistently formatted output when instructions alone are not enough.
More emphasis on the same descriptions rarely fixes differences in interpretation; the model needs to see what correct output looks like.
Regex can strip numbering, but it cannot reliably split merged outcomes or undo paraphrasing; it patches symptoms downstream.
A larger model may follow instructions somewhat better, but the cheaper and more direct fix for format consistency is examples.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, extracted data feeds a "partner university profile" read by the partnerships team. It combines tuition and fee figures per program, recent news about accreditation decisions, and the technical rules of each university's credit system (quarter versus semester units, conversion factors). Today every section is rendered as one uniform bullet list, and readers say fee comparisons and conversion rules are hard to use. Which output design is best?
opcoes: Keep one bullet-list format for every section, so that readers and any downstream parser can rely on the same predictable structure throughout.
Render every section as narrative prose, so that the profile reads naturally and the fee figures appear in context instead of in isolation.
Render fees as tables, accreditation news as short prose, and credit-system rules as step-by-step lists, so each content type is easy to use.
Render every section as JSON inside the profile, so that the partnerships team and downstream systems can consume exactly the same output.
questoes.explicacao: Different content types are easiest to use in different forms: financial figures in tables for comparison, news as prose for narrative context, and technical rules as structured lists. Forcing everything into one uniform format makes some sections harder to read and compare.
feedbacks: Uniformity helps parsers, but this profile is for people; a bulleted list of fees makes comparisons across programs hard, which is exactly the complaint.
Prose suits the news, but fee figures buried in sentences are hard to compare, and conversion rules lose their step-by-step structure.
Correct. Render each content type in the form that fits it: tables, prose, or structured lists.
JSON serves systems, not readers; downstream systems should consume the structured extraction directly, not a human-facing profile.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, the agent has `parse_grade_table` (description: "Parses a grade table") and `parse_grading_policy` (description: "Parses grading information"). On transcripts, the agent calls `parse_grading_policy` instead of `parse_grade_table` in about 18% of cases and returns an empty policy object. The team wants reliable selection between the two without adding a routing layer. What should change?
opcoes: Add an explicit system-prompt rule, "use parse_grade_table for transcripts", so that the model maps each document type to its tool.
Rewrite both descriptions to state what each parses, its expected input and output, and when to use it instead of the other tool.
Merge them into one `parse_grades` tool with a `mode` parameter, so that the model only picks a mode rather than a tool.
Add programmatic input checks that reject grade tables sent to `parse_grading_policy`, so the model gets an error and retries.
questoes.explicacao: Tool descriptions are the main signal the model uses to choose a tool, and these two are nearly indistinguishable. Rewriting them to state purpose, expected inputs (rows of course grades versus prose about grading rules), outputs, and when to prefer each over the other directly addresses the misrouting.
feedbacks: Keyword rules in the system prompt can misfire (transcripts often include a grading-policy legend) and work around weak descriptions instead of fixing them.
Correct. Clear, differentiated descriptions are the primary mechanism for reliable tool selection.
Merging is a valid design choice, but it moves the same ambiguity into the `mode` parameter and is more work than fixing the descriptions.
Rejection makes the error visible, but each mistake still costs a failed call and a retry; it catches misrouting instead of preventing it.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, a validation loop retries failed transcript extractions up to three times, sending the specific validation errors back each time. Retries fix 94% of date-format errors. But for 7% of transcripts, the required `institution_accreditation_id` fails validation on every attempt, coming back as a different invented ID or as null. Reviewers checking 20 of these found that the transcripts name the institution, while partners upload accreditation letters separately. What most likely explains the difference?
opcoes: The retry prompt does not include the specific validation error for the ID field, so the model cannot tell what it needs to correct there.
Three attempts are too few for a field this complex; raising the limit to six would give the model time to converge on a valid ID.
The ID is absent from the transcript itself, so feedback cannot produce it; retries help with format and structure errors, not missing data.
The ID field is free text in the schema; adding a regex pattern for valid IDs would let the retries converge on a correctly formed value.
questoes.explicacao: Retry-with-error-feedback works when the information is in the document and the problem is format or structure, as with the dates. When the value exists only in another document that was not provided, no feedback can make it appear; the fix is to supply that document, or to make the field nullable and route the case for follow-up.
feedbacks: The same loop sends specific errors for dates and fixes 94% of them; the ID failures persist for a different reason.
More attempts produce more invented IDs; the information the model needs is not in the input.
Correct. Retries are ineffective when the required information is not in the source document.
A pattern would make invented IDs look valid, which is worse; the model still has no source for the real value.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, two workflows were moved to the Message Batches API to cut costs, with results polled every 30 seconds. In the first, a student uploads a transcript during the credit-transfer application, and the page waits to show the estimated transferable credits. In the second, all syllabi updated during the week are re-extracted on Sunday night for the catalog. Since the change, students report being stuck on "Analyzing your transcript..." for hours. What is the flaw?
opcoes: The polling interval is too long; polling every 5 seconds would surface finished transcript results quickly enough for the student who is waiting.
Each transcript batch is too small to be processed efficiently; grouping 500 uploads per batch before submitting would make results arrive sooner.
The transcript extraction blocks a waiting student and needs the synchronous API; only the weekly syllabus re-extraction fits the batch API.
Both should stay on the batch API, with the transcript page replaced by an email sent when results arrive, so students are not left waiting.
questoes.explicacao: The Message Batches API trades latency for cost: results can take up to 24 hours, with no SLA. That suits latency-tolerant workloads like the weekly re-extraction, but not a blocking step in which a student is waiting on the page; that step needs the synchronous API.
feedbacks: Polling more often only detects completion sooner; it cannot make the batch finish sooner, and processing can take hours.
Grouping uploads makes each student also wait for other students' uploads, and batch size does not create a latency guarantee.
Correct. Match the API to latency needs: synchronous for blocking steps, batch for overnight or weekly work.
This changes the product to fit the API: the student needs the estimate while applying, and an email up to a day later breaks that flow.

questoes.pergunta: Coursewell's extraction system also powers a registrar assistant. In one long conversation, a registrar works through four credit-transfer applications, each with an application ID, disputed credits, and a status. After about 40 turns, the assistant attributed APP-2291's 9 disputed credits to APP-2304. The team then added an "open applications" block, with one structured entry per application ID holding its credits and status, maintained outside the conversation history and included in every request. The mix-ups stopped. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: Keeping per-application facts in a separate layer outside the history kept them intact, so details no longer blended across applications.
The gain came mainly from a shorter prompt, since the structured block replaced the conversation history that the model had been receiving.
The mix-ups were caused by the extraction schema, and the block helped only because it re-validated each application's fields on every turn.
The block worked because the model reads JSON more carefully than prose; formatting the whole history as JSON would have had the same effect.
questoes.explicacao: In multi-issue sessions, details of different items blend together as the conversation grows. Extracting each item's key data (IDs, amounts, statuses) into a separate structured context layer, included in each request, keeps those facts distinct and current, while the full conversation history is still sent for coherence.
feedbacks: Correct. Persisting structured per-issue data in a separate context layer prevents mix-ups in multi-issue sessions.
The block is added alongside the history, not substituted for it; the full conversation still needs to be sent for coherence.
Nothing points to the extraction schema; the facts were right early in the conversation and blurred as it grew.
Format alone does not keep the facts apart; a 40-turn history in JSON would still bury each application's details in a long context.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, Pydantic validation rejects about 5% of syllabus extractions: `credit_hours` comes back as "3-4" instead of a number, or `prerequisites` comes back as a sentence instead of a list of course codes. Today a failure simply re-runs the original prompt. A developer proposes that the retry send only the failed JSON with the instruction "fix the validation errors". How should you evaluate the proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: the failed JSON is enough, because the errors are visible in the values that the model itself produced on its first attempt.
Improve it: include the source document, the rejected output, and each specific error message, so that fixes are checked against the source.
Reject it: keep re-running the original prompt, since a fresh attempt without the failed output avoids anchoring on its earlier mistakes.
Improve it: send the specific errors with the original prompt but leave out the failed JSON, so that the model re-extracts without anchoring.
questoes.explicacao: Effective retry-with-error-feedback includes three things: the original document (to re-check values against the source), the failed extraction (what to correct), and the specific validation errors (what is wrong). Without the source, the model can only reshape values like "3-4" blindly; without the errors, it does not know what to fix.
feedbacks: Without the syllabus, the model cannot check what "3-4" should become (for example, a variable-credit course), and a vague instruction does not name the errors.
Correct. Include the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors.
A blind re-run repeats the conditions that produced the error; specific feedback is what guides the correction.
Including the errors is right, but dropping the failed output makes the model start over instead of making targeted corrections to its previous attempt.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, each document must first go through `extract_course_metadata` (institution, course code, term), because the enrichment tools `lookup_catalog_equivalent` and `convert_credit_system` depend on that metadata. With `tool_choice` set to "auto", in 11% of runs the model calls `lookup_catalog_equivalent` first, with guessed metadata. The tools must stay as they are, and the model should still decide which enrichment tools to call afterwards. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Force `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_course_metadata"}` on the first request, then handle the enrichment steps in follow-up turns.
Set `tool_choice` to "any" for the whole conversation, so that every turn ends in a tool call and metadata extraction cannot be skipped.
Force `extract_course_metadata` on every request in the conversation, so that the metadata is refreshed before each enrichment call.
Keep "auto" and move `extract_course_metadata` to the top of the tools list, so that the model considers it first when choosing a tool.
questoes.explicacao: Forced tool selection guarantees that a specific tool runs, so forcing `extract_course_metadata` on the first request ensures metadata extraction happens before enrichment. Subsequent turns can then let the model choose the enrichment tools. "any" guarantees some tool call, but not which one.
feedbacks: Correct. Force the prerequisite tool first, then process the subsequent steps in follow-up turns.
"any" guarantees a tool call but lets the model choose which one, so it can still start with `lookup_catalog_equivalent`.
Forcing the same tool on every request means the enrichment tools can never be called.
The order of the tools list is not a reliable control over which tool the model calls first.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, a "transfer justification" for each course combines findings from the partner's syllabus, the catalog entry, and an accreditation report. An intermediate step condenses the findings before the final write-up. A university audit rejected several justifications because a claim such as "covers 85% of the target course's learning outcomes" could not be traced to any specific document. Which two changes best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Remove the condensing step and pass all extracted text to the final write-up, so nothing is compressed and every source stays in context.
Have each extraction step output every claim as a record with its source document, page, and the excerpt that supports it.
Require the condensing step to keep each claim linked to its document, page, and excerpt, merging those links instead of dropping them.
Keep only claims that at least two sources support during condensing, so that every claim left in the justification is well attributed.
Build claim-source records after the write-up by matching each final sentence to its most similar source passage, so auditors can trace it.
questoes.explicacao: Attribution is lost when findings are compressed without keeping the link between each claim and its source. Producing structured claim-source mappings at extraction time, and requiring later steps to preserve and merge them, keeps every claim traceable to a document, page, and excerpt all the way to the final justification.
feedbacks: Passing everything avoids compression but floods the write-up's context, and the final text still would not tie each claim to its source.
Correct. Structured claim-source mappings are created where the evidence is read.
Correct. Downstream steps must preserve and merge the mappings, or attribution is lost during summarization.
Filtering discards valid single-source claims and still does not record which sources support each remaining claim.
Attribution reconstructed by similarity after the fact is a guess: a condensed claim like "85% of outcomes" may match the wrong passage or none, so the mapping must be kept from extraction onward.

questoes.pergunta: In Coursewell's extraction system, a validation agent checks that each extracted course code exists in the partner's catalog. Today every check goes back to the coordinator, which calls the catalog agent and then re-invokes validation, adding two round trips per document. Logs show that about 90% of checks are exact lookups ("does code X exist for institution Y in term Z?"), while 10% need fuzzy matching for renamed or merged courses. Which design best reduces overhead while keeping the system reliable?
opcoes: Give the validation agent a scoped `course_code_exists` lookup tool, and keep sending fuzzy matching through the coordinator to the catalog agent.
Give the validation agent all of the catalog agent's tools, so that it can resolve exact lookups and fuzzy matches without any round trips.
Merge the validation and catalog agents into one agent, so that code checks and fuzzy matching happen in one context without handoffs.
Have the catalog agent export the full catalog to a file before validation starts, so that the validation agent can search it with Grep.
questoes.explicacao: A scoped cross-role tool covers the frequent, simple case (exact existence checks) directly in the validation agent, removing most round trips. Complex cases that need the catalog agent's specialized matching still go through the coordinator, preserving separation of concerns and observability.
feedbacks: Correct. Provide a narrowly scoped cross-role tool for the high-frequency need and keep complex cases on the coordinator path.
This over-provisions the validation agent with tools outside its role, inviting the misuse that scoped access prevents.
Merging removes handoffs but creates one agent with a broader toolset and mixed responsibilities, which degrades tool selection.
A pre-exported catalog avoids calls but can be stale for the current term and turns lookups into text searches over a dump.
